author: caidéiseach

kp.k: AI threatens the junior-labour economics of professional services
kp.d: The author argues that law, accounting and consulting firms traditionally exchange partners’ expertise and client relationships for juniors’ routine labour, generating profits while training future partners. Generative AI threatens this arrangement by performing entry-level tasks. The document cites Goldman Sachs’ estimate that up to 300 million full-time jobs worldwide could face some automation exposure, rather than reporting that many job losses.
qs: partners exchange their knowledge and client relationships for the labour of juniors.
The pyramid works because the bottom is wide: you need lots of junior people to handle the volume of routine work.
AI could expose up to 300 million full-time jobs worldwide to some degree of automation.

kp.k: Reported staffing trends suggest a narrower associate base
kp.d: The document cites a 2025 Thomson Reuters analysis reporting that associates’ share of law firm attorneys declined from 44.5% to 40.2% over 15 years, while non-equity partners and counsel gained share. The author interprets this as evidence of compression toward a diamond staffing structure; the reported figures themselves describe changes in composition, not an identified AI causal effect.
qs: associates now make up a smaller proportion of law firm attorneys than they did 15 years ago (down from 44.5% to 40.2%), while the share of senior lawyers (non-equity partners and counsel) has grown.
The classic pyramid is morphing into something more diamond-shaped: narrower at the bottom, wider in the middle, and still narrow at the top.

kp.k: Automation examples span legal work and investment banking
kp.d: The author cites reports of a 40% reduction in human contract reviews and Allen & Overy’s deployment of Harvey AI to all 3,500 lawyers for drafting and research. As a cross-industry analogy, the document reports that Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were considering cutting analyst hiring by two-thirds, not that these cuts had occurred. The author also asserts that mundane tasks constituted 70-80% of entry-level staff work.

kp.k: The AI Slide threatens foundational learning and verification
kp.d: The author’s 'AI Slide' framework argues that removing beginner tasks also removes the cognitive processes through which expertise develops. Proposed risks include weak fundamentals, difficulty connecting advanced concepts to prior knowledge, inflated perceptions of competence from lightly editing AI output, and inadequate human checking of complex output without experience performing the underlying work. These are presented as mechanisms and concerns, not measured learning outcomes.

kp.k: Simulation and tiered AI training offer alternative formation
kp.d: The document reports Goodwin Procter’s intensive 8-week simulation-based training for new associates, using mock transactions and lawsuits to substitute high-quality practice for routine-work volume. It also reports PwC’s mandatory AI training for all 75,000 U.S. employees beginning in 2023, with tiers from basic literacy to advanced technical skills. PwC limited the programme to 5 months because of rapid technological change, according to the cited Chief People Officer.

The author extends this vision to legal and consulting services, asserting that solo attorneys already use AI to run practices and that boutique principals plus AI perform work formerly requiring ten people, without naming examples. In this model, human strategy, quality control and relationships remain central while AI supplies execution.

The author allows that the diamond may be transitional, while maintaining that firms are moving away from pyramids and must reinvent professional learning.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The author argues that AI is replacing routine junior work, compressing professional-services staffing pyramids into diamonds, and disrupting the apprenticeship through which firms develop expertise.
pts.d: Across law, accounting and consulting, the author claims that generative AI can perform the routine work previously assigned to graduates and associates, reducing demand for entry-level staff. The predicted staffing diamond has fewer juniors, a wider middle of experienced practitioners exercising judgment, maintaining client relationships and directing AI, and a narrow leadership tier. The author also predicts fewer management layers as AI handles coordination, oversight and analysis. A distinct claim concerns professional development: removing repetitive foundational work weakens learning, can create an illusion of competence, and makes human verification of sophisticated AI outputs harder for inexperienced practitioners. Proposed responses include simulation-based practice, baseline AI literacy, and earlier expectations of critical thinking, communication and ethical judgment. Separately, the author presents AI-enabled solo practices and small consultancies as a model in which a human retains strategy, quality control and relationships while AI executes work at scale. The 'personal diamond' is this human-centred arrangement of AI systems, distinct from the firm's staffing diamond.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The author supports the argument with reported staffing data, adoption and training examples, secondary reports, and forecasts by outside authorities; several broader claims are presented without a specified empirical basis.
pts.d: The author cites a 2025 Thomson Reuters analysis reporting that associates' share of law-firm attorneys fell from 44.5% to 40.2% over 15 years while non-equity partners and counsel increased, presenting this as evidence of compression. Other cited support includes reports of a 40% reduction in human contract reviews and Allen & Overy's deployment of Harvey, the legal-AI product, to 3,500 lawyers. The author draws a financial-services parallel from reports that Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were considering cutting analyst hiring by two-thirds; this is described as contemplated hiring change rather than a completed reduction. For the training argument, the author cites Casey Flaherty's discussion of associate development, Goodwin Procter's eight-week simulation programme, and PwC's mandatory, tiered AI training for 75,000 US employees. The PwC programme is described as lasting five months because of rapid technological evolution. Supporting forecasts quoted or paraphrased by the author include Goldman Sachs's estimate that up to 300 million full-time jobs could be exposed to some automation, Bill Gates's broad ten-year prediction, Jamie Dimon's automation forecast, Gartner's organisational-flattening forecast, and Sam Altman's one-person-company prediction. These are outside authorities invoked by the blog author, not interviews conducted in the document. The assertion that mundane tasks accounted for 70–80% of entry-level work has no separately specified measurement basis. The cognitive-learning claims and examples of solo attorneys or one-person consultancies replacing larger teams are not accompanied by named studies or identified practices.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The author presents compression as already occurring in 2025, predicts further restructuring in the near future, and acknowledges qualifications concerning AI capabilities, retained human work and new job creation.
pts.d: The historical staffing comparison covers the 15 years preceding the cited 2025 analysis and is used to support a present-tense transformation argument. The author describes AI literacy as a baseline in 2025 and suggests that work considered mid-level in 2017 might become entry-level by 2027. The diamond firm is a near-future prediction, conditional on AI handling enough routine work to reduce junior staffing needs. The training dilemma is illustrated conditionally: if AI handles 80% of the work through which juniors traditionally learn, firms must change training. The author cites Gartner's prediction that by 2026, 20% of organisations will use AI to flatten structures and eliminate more than half of current middle-management positions. Other horizons are less specific: Dimon's forecast concerns the coming years, Altman's one-person AI unicorns are expected 'soon', and Gates's prediction concerns the next ten years. The author acknowledges, through cited outside commentary, limitations in current AI's common sense and complex real-world interaction, reasons people may continue doing work for enjoyment or creativity, and the possibility of technology creating new jobs. The diamond may therefore be transitional, although the author remains firm about movement away from pyramidal staffing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes chiefly affect graduates and junior professionals, experienced practitioners, managers, partners, training functions, and AI-enabled solo or boutique providers.
pts.d: Graduates, junior lawyers, accounting staff and financial analysts face fewer entry-level openings, less routine practice, and higher starting skill requirements. Experienced professionals become more central to judgment, client communication and human verification of AI outputs, while management roles devoted to coordination and oversight may shrink. Partners and senior leaders retain strategy and valuable client relationships, but the traditional exchange of partner knowledge and relationships for junior labour changes. Law firms and other professional-services organisations must redesign development pathways rather than rely on high volumes of routine billable work. Goodwin Procter and PwC illustrate training responses in law and accounting respectively; the Big Four references here primarily concern accounting and professional services, not specifically their legal-service arms. Solo attorneys and boutique consultancies are presented as beneficiaries of expanded delivery capacity, with one practitioner potentially doing work previously requiring a team. Clients remain the recipients of human relationship management and AI-supported execution, but the document does not offer a concrete prediction about legal fees, access to justice or outcomes for the public.
